title: Misinformation, Conspiracies & AI Persuasion
description: Explore familiarity mistaken for truth through dialogue, evidence and psychological reasoning.

lessons.title: I've seen it everywhere
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of familiarity mistaken for truth.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Repetition can increase perceived truth because a familiar statement is processed more easily. Several forwards of one screenshot do not provide independent checks. The important investigative task is tracing an assertion back to its origin and then finding evidence that does not rely on that same source.

A repeated claim can still be true. Familiarity is not evidence for truth or falsity by itself.
nodes.sources: Fazio et al. (2015), Knowledge Does Not Protect Against Illusory Truth.

nodes.explanation: The trigger is several people forward the same screenshot. Its possible meaning is ivo reads repeated appearance as widespread corroboration. The protective behaviour may contribute to a longer-term cost: copied assertions acquire the appearance of an independent evidence base.
nodes.counterexample: A repeated claim can still be true. Familiarity is not evidence for truth or falsity by itself.

lessons.title: What would change your mind?
lessons.teach: An initial explanation is useful only if it can be challenged. Revisit the characters, test a rival account and apply the idea in another setting. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Test an account of familiarity mistaken for truth with new evidence and transfer it to a new case.
